co_01_piggy_bank.blurb: Piggy Bank is a short stretch of limestone at The Bank, one of the busiest cliffs on Shelf Road north of Canon City. Nearly everything is bolted face and crack climbing on sharp holds, with grades spread from the 5.8s through the low 5.12s and the heart of it around 5.9 to 5.11. Flesh Tuxedo, Number 1 Super Guy and Puking Yuppies are among the favorites. The cliff band holds warm rock, which makes it a good pick on cold, bright days, but it gets crowded and the easier routes have polished from traffic. Expect the trail down to the base to be slick when wet or icy.
co_01_piggy_bank.parking_note: Drive up the rough dirt road to The Bank campground and use its day-use lot, which has pit toilets. Park there and not along the road. The road is steep and bumpy, so large trailers are a poor idea.

co_redgarden_lumpe_to_the_top.blurb: This is the upper, left-hand part of Redgarden Wall in Eldorado Canyon, from Lumpe Tower up past the Middle Tower to the Hot Spur. Climbing is almost entirely traditional and multi-pitch on sandstone, with some broken sections and an adventurous, route-finding feel; sound gear skills matter more here than at a sport crag. Grades run from easy fifth class through 5.14, concentrated between about 5.7 and 5.11. Rebuffat's Arete, Rewritten and The Green Spur are well-known lines. Few rappel routes exist, so plan your descent before leaving the ground, and note that some lines stay in shade until late morning.
co_redgarden_lumpe_to_the_top.parking_note: Use the lot at the east end of the state park, then walk uphill a short way to the footbridge and cross it. Weekends can fill the canyon, so arrive early.

co_radio_head.blurb: Radio Head is a southwest-facing granite crag at Devil's Head in the South Platte area, reached by one of the shorter walks at the area. Sport and trad share the cliff, with about half the routes needing gear, and grades run from moderate up to the low 5.13s, with the bulk between 5.10 and 5.12. Giant Dihedral, The Bends and Surefire show the range. Most routes get afternoon sun, and a 60 m rope is usually needed to lower off. Plan on a small rack of nuts and cams for the trad lines.
co_radio_head.parking_note: Take Rampart Range Road past the campground turnoff and continue uphill to the radio towers. Park in the larger pullout a little way down the road from the towers rather than at the towers themselves.
co_radio_head.approach: From the radio towers, head northwest along the ridge, keeping below the crest on its west side. After passing a large cluster of quartz crystals, descend cairned slabs to the base of the cliff.

co_lost_angel.blurb: Lost Angel is the largest piece of granite in the Upper Dream Canyon area above Boulder, with routes from one to several pitches. Bolts are the main protection, with a good number of trad lines mixed in, and grades cluster from 5.10 through 5.12 with a handful of easier and harder outliers. Archangel, Earth Voyage and Divination are among the better-known climbs. The rock is big and routes can be hard to find at first, so expect some route-finding. Some starts get awkward during spring runoff, and the road in is dirt and not obvious, so go with directions.
co_lost_angel.parking_note: From Boulder Canyon, turn onto Sugarloaf Road, then follow the dirt Lost Angel Road to a small dirt lot. Space is limited and neighbors live nearby, so keep noise down and pack out everything.
co_lost_angel.approach: Follow the obvious trail south from the lot, then drop around the formation through a notch and down a gully. If the ground begins to feel like fifth class, you have gone too far.

co_twin_owls_2.blurb: The Twin Owls are the best-known rock formation on Lumpy Ridge, visible from much of Estes Park and set on the northern edge of Rocky Mountain National Park. The granite is technical, with flared cracks, thin seams and faint features that demand good footwork, and protection on the harder lines can be thin. Climbing is mostly traditional multi-pitch with a smattering of aid, and grades center on 5.8 through 5.11. Crack of Fear, Wolf's Tooth and Tiger's Tooth are popular. The formations are close to the trailhead and busier on weekends.
co_twin_owls_2.parking_note: Drive north from Estes Park to the Lumpy Ridge trailhead at the end of Lumpy Ridge Road, where a paved lot serves the ridge. It is a longer walk to the Owls than from the older lot.

co_menses_prow.blurb: Menses Prow is a horseshoe-shaped limestone cliff in The Gallery at Shelf Road, a favorite for its mix of sun and shade and its fairly secluded feel. Nearly all of it is bolted face climbing, with a few trad lines, and most grades fall between 5.10 and 5.12 with a good supply of moderates as well. First Blood, Menses and Sundogs are favorites, and a sub-area known for easy climbs suits newer leaders. The rock is sharp and some holds are polished, and the popular lines fill quickly on good days, so arrive early.
co_menses_prow.parking_note: Park in the day-use area at the Sand Gulch campground off Garden Park Road, and begin the walk from there.
co_menses_prow.approach: Follow the trail from the lot, staying straight at the signed turn for the Far Side. At the next signed junction take the left fork toward the prow, cross the wash, and climb switchbacks up the steep slope to the cliff.

co_cracked_canyon.blurb: Cracked Canyon is a small gorge above the town of Ophir, west of Telluride, holding traditional crack and face climbing. Routes are around 80 feet long, with grades from easy to hard, though most fall between 5.8 and 5.11, plus a top-rope. Cello, Javelin and Orange Peel are among the classics. The canyon floor is shaded, the talus approach is steep, and loose rock is common, so go carefully and watch for people below. Bring a standard trad rack.
co_cracked_canyon.parking_note: Pull off at the roadside spots below the canyon in Ophir, roughly 100 yards beyond the post office.
co_cracked_canyon.approach: Find the climbers' trail through the forest and up the steep talus slope, heading for the canyon just right of the main wall. Loose rock is common, so avoid kicking stones down onto others.
